column1: ## AMR cohort -- S. aureus specimens callable at the paper's >=20x threshold
## Selected from Street et al. Table S3 (catalogue/street2022_table_s3.tsv),
## not from raw sequencing yield. Yield turned out to be a poor proxy for
## S. aureus content: of the six highest-yield saponin runs, only two
## Inclusion: sequencing_species == Staphylococcus aureus AND the authors'
## own mean reference depth >= 20x, which is the threshold they required for
## a resistance-SNP call. Their depth is a good predictor of ours since we
## map the same reads to the same reference, but it is not identical --
## re-derive depth from our own BAMs before calling, do not trust this column.
## ENA patient_N == Table S3 sample N. Verified on six specimens by matching
## total non-human base counts to within 0.01% (e.g. sample 119: S3
## 7,350,065,534 vs ENA 7,349,284,900 -- the gap is reads dropped at deposit).
## Where a patient has several saponin runs, the highest-yield one is marked
## primary and the others replicate. Replicates are a free check on
## variant-call stability: same specimen, same prep, independent library.
## Sample 41 is the regression test. Street et al. missed a resistant rpoB
## A477V present in ~20% of reads there, because their pipeline took consensus
## calls and did not model mixed populations. A477V IS in our Gordon catalogue
## (rifampicin, MIC 1). Clair3 reports allele fractions, so if our arm is
## working it should see what theirs could not. If we also miss it, the
## reproduction has inherited the flaw rather than fixed it.
## Columns: run  patient  prep  reads  bases  s3_depth  s3_cov1x  role
## marginal = depth near the 20x floor (samples 20, 13) or poor breadth
## (sample 117 at 43% 1x coverage). Expect many drug-organism combinations
## here to land in "insufficient coverage" rather than a call. That is the
## correct outcome, not a failure -- 60 of the paper's 152 combinations did
## the same. Do NOT collapse insufficient-coverage into susceptible.
